source_text: Καὶ δῆτα τὴν ἡσυχίαν ἄγειν ἀσφαλὲς καταφαίνεται, μή πῃ προφάσει μὲν εὐχαριστίας, ὑπὸ δὲ προπετείας ἴσως περὶ σεμνῶν καὶ ἱερῶν ἄσεμνά τε καὶ εὐτελῆ καὶ καταπεπατημένα διεξιὼν, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐφικνῶμαι τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθαιρῶ τι, τό γε ἐπ᾽ ἐμοὶ, παρὰ τοῖς οὕτως ἔχειν πιστεύουσιν, ὡς ἀσθενὴς ὢν ὁ λόγος περιυβρίζων μᾶλλον, ἤπερ ἐξομοιούμενος τοῖς ἔργοις τῇ δυνάμει ὑποτυπώσεται. καίτοι τὰ μὲν σὰ, ἀκαθαίρετα καὶ ἀνύβριστα, ὦ φίλη κεφαλὴ, καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον τὰ θεῖα μένοντα ἑαυτῶν, ὡς ἔχει, ἀσάλευτα, οὐδὲν βλαπτόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν μικρῶν καὶ ἀναξίων ἡμετέρων λόγων. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως τὴν τῆς θρασύτητος καὶ προπετείας δόξαν διαφευξόμεθα, ἐπιπηδήσαντες ὑπ᾽ ἀνοίας, μικρῷ καὶ νῷ, καὶ παρασκευῇ, μεγάλοις καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς ἴσως πράγμασι. καὶ εἰ μὲν ἀλλαχόθι που καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἄλλων τοιαῦτα προεθυμήθημεν νεανιεύσασθαι, θρασεῖς μὲν καὶ οὕτως ἦμεν καὶ πλημμελεῖς τινες. οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀναίδεια τῆς προπετείας αἰτία, τῷ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ ταῦτα θρασύνεσθαι. νυνὶ δὲ πᾶν τὸ μέτρον τῆς ἀνοίας ἀποπλήσομεν, ἢ καὶ ἀπεπλήσαμεν ἤδη, ἐπεμβαίνειν τολμήσαντες ἀνίπτοις τοῖς ποσὶ, τοῦτο δὴ τὸ τοῦ λόγου, ἀκοαῖς αἷς αὐτὸς ὁ θεῖος λόγος οὐδὲν ἐσκεπασμένοις, ὡς ταῖς τῶν πολλῶν ἀνθρώπων, τοῖς ποσὶν, ὥσπερ ὑπὸ παχέων τινῶν δερμάτων τῶν αἰνιγματωδῶν καὶ ἀσαφῶν λέξεων, ἀλλὰ γυμνοῖς, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, σαφὴς καὶ πρόδηλος ἐμβατεύων ἐπιδημεῖ. ἡμεῖς δὲ ὥσπερ ῥύπον ἢ πηλόν τινα τοὺς ἀνθρωπίνους ἡμῶν λόγους φέροντες, ἐπαντλεῖν ἐτολμήσαμεν ἀκοαῖς θείων καὶ καθαρῶν ἀκούειν μεμελετηκυίαις φωνῶν. ἆρ᾽ οὖν ἀπόχρη μέχρι τούτου ἁμαρτεῖν, καὶ νῦν γοῦν σωφρονεῖν ἄρξασθαι χρὴ, μηκέτι μὲν περαιτέρω προβαίνοντας τῷ λόγῳ, αὐτοῦ δὲ καταπαύσαντας; ἐβουλόμην μέν· οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἅπαξ μοι θρασυνομένῳ, ἐξέστω τὴν αἰτίαν πρῶτον εἰπεῖν, ὑφ᾽ ἧς ἐναχθεὶς ἐπὶ τοῦτον ἧκα τὸν ἀγῶνα, εἴ πῃ καὶ συγγνώμη γένοιτό μοι τῆς προπετείας ταύτης.
thought_title: Afraid to walk into sacred hearing with unwashed feet
orientation: Gregory fears that a weak speech would insult holy things, yet resolves to explain why he has dared to speak.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed to keep quiet appears safe, lest by pretext of thanksgiving but through rashness perhaps, going through about solemn and holy things undignified, cheap and trodden down, trite, I not only fail to reach truth, but also pull down, detract something, as far as on me, among those believing it is so, as a weak λόγος will sketch outraging rather than matching the deeds in power. Yet yours are not to be destroyed and not to be insulted, dear head, and much more divine things remaining as they are unshaken, harmed in nothing by our small, unworthy words. But we, I know not how we shall escape the reputation of boldness and rashness, having leapt upon through folly, with small mind and preparation, great things perhaps beyond us. And if elsewhere and before others we had been eager to act youthfully, show off, bold even so we were and faulty. Nevertheless shamelessness of the rashness cause [sense: would not be], by not being bold before you. Now we shall fill up the whole measure of ἄνοια, or already filled, having dared to step in with unwashed feet, as the saying goes, into ears/hearing in which the divine Word himself — not with covered feet as in those of most men, as by thick hides of riddling and obscure words, but bare, as one might say — clear and manifest walking dwells, sojourns. We, carrying like filth or mud our human words, dared to pour onto ears practiced to hear divine and pure voices. Is it enough to have erred this far, and now at least must begin to be sensible, no further advancing in speech, but stopping here? I would wish; nevertheless, once being bold, let it be allowed to say first the cause by which led on I came to this contest, if somehow pardon may come to me for this προπέτεια.

pass_b_english: And so it seems safe to keep quiet. Otherwise, on the pretext of giving thanks but in truth perhaps out of rashness, I might say undignified, cheap and trite things about solemn and holy matters, and not only fail to reach the truth, but even, as far as lies in me, take something away from them in the minds of those who believe these things are so. For a weak speech will sketch them by insulting them rather than by matching the deeds in power. And yet what is yours, dear friend, cannot be torn down or insulted; and much more do divine things remain as they are, unshaken, not harmed at all by our small and unworthy words. But I do not know how we shall escape a name for boldness and rashness, having leapt in our folly, with small mind and small preparation, upon great matters, perhaps beyond us.

If we had been eager to show off like this elsewhere and before other people, we would have been bold even so, and somewhat at fault. Yet the rashness would not have been put down to shamelessness, since the bold venture would not have been made in your presence. Now, however, we shall fill up the whole measure of folly, or have filled it already, for we have dared to step, as the saying goes, with unwashed feet into ears where the divine Word himself makes his home. He does not walk there as he walks in the ears of most people, with his feet covered, as it were, by thick hides of riddling and obscure words. He walks there with bare feet, so to speak, clear and plain. And we, carrying our human words like filth or mud, have dared to pour them into ears trained to hear divine and pure voices.

Is it enough, then, to have gone wrong this far? Must we now at least begin to be sensible, and go no further with the speech, but stop here? I would like to. Yet since I have once been bold, let me be allowed first to state the cause that led me into this contest, in the hope that I may be pardoned for this rashness.
notes: The print 'οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀναίδεια τῆς προπετείας αἰτία, τῷ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ ταῦτα θρασύνεσθαι' does not construe well. The English follows the sense of the Vossius Latin column ('sed tamen impudentiae tribuenda temeritas ... quod non coram te talia auderemus', partly lost in the scan): the rashness would not count as shamelessness, because it would not be ventured in Origen's presence; this also fits the contrast with 'νυνὶ δέ' ('Now, however'). Doubtful reading. 'With unwashed feet' (ἀνίπτοις τοῖς ποσί) is marked by Gregory himself as a proverb ('as the saying goes'; Latin margin 'Proverb.'), not Scripture. The bare feet of the Word may recall Exodus 3:5, but the image is Gregory's own; not cited. ὁ θεῖος λόγος is capitalized as 'the divine Word' since Gregory speaks of the Word dwelling in Origen's hearing. 'Dear friend' renders ὦ φίλη κεφαλή ('dear head'), a Greek idiom of affection; 'what is yours' renders the bare τὰ σά (Latin 'tua quidem omnia'). The Latin column for the doubtful clause was checked on the page image (PDF 75): 'tamen impudentiae tribuenda temeritas non esset, quòd non coram te talia auderemus'.
